prompt: Draw on the metaphysics-of-emergence and virtual-reality literature to theorize how Aristotelian phantasia might illuminate the phenomenology of virtual perception.

result.content:
## 1. Phantasia and Aisthesis: Perception, Imagination, and the Problem of Appearance The relationship between φαντασία and αἴσθησις constitutes one of the most vexed problems in Aristotle's philosophy of mind, precisely because phantasia is at once causally dependent on perception and yet irreducible to it. As Aristotle establishes in *De Anima* III.3, phantasia is defined as a κίνησις resulting from an actual exercise of sense-perception, such that imagination cannot occur without the prior operation of the senses; indeed, as White observes, among the decisive points of distinction is "that an 'appearing' (phainetai) may occur when the sense-powers are inoperative, as in dreams or when one's eyes are closed, so that phantasia cannot be the same thing as sensation" (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, pp. 12–14). This observation establishes a fundamental contrast: while αἴσθησις requires the actual presence of a sensible object that moves the faculty from potentiality to actuality, phantasia can operate in the absence of such an object, generating appearances that possess quasi-perceptual vividness without immediate sensory grounding. Accordingly, Frede argues that Aristotle's indirect, negative method of distinguishing phantasia from sense-perception in *De Anima* III.3 is strategically motivated, insofar as he wishes to secure agreement that phantasia differs from perception before revealing that it possesses no independent faculty or objects of its own (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 3). This is significant for any theorization of virtual perception, since the virtual environment similarly furnishes appearances without the ordinary causal chains of natural perception. Hawhee further illuminates this dynamic by situating phantasia's relationship to suasion and desire, noting the passage where Aristotle explains that people "desire to see and possess many things after hearing about them" (Hawhee 2011, p. [PAGE NEEDED]). The rhetorical dimension thus reveals that phantasia mediates between bare sensory reception and a richer perceptual engagement shaped by desire; a graded relationship between sensory phantasia and deliberative phantasia—the latter involving belief and calculative reasoning—will be elaborated in subsequent sections. For the present analysis, what matters is that phantasia's contrast with aisthesis opens a phenomenological space in which virtual appearances may function analogously to natural sense-impressions while remaining ontologically distinct from them. 

## 2. Phantasma and Phantasia: The Image and Its Cognitive Function If phantasia names the movement or faculty, the φάντασμα names its product—the quasi-perceptual image that persists after sensation ceases and furnishes the content upon which thought itself depends. Heidegger captures this crucial relationship when he glosses phantasia as "the 'making-present-to-itself' of the world," observing that even νοεῖν—thorough deliberation about matters not perceptually present—"is something like a φαντασία or cannot be without φαντασία, then thinking too could not be without standing in the context of the entire life of a human being" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 149). This passage is decisive, for it situates the phantasma not as a mere epiphenomenal residue of sensation but as the indispensable medium through which human cognition engages with what is absent, past, or merely possible. Indeed, Frede notes that "phantasiai here have been degraded to mere epiphenomena, the lingering after-images of sensations," only to contest this reductive reading by pointing to Aristotle's own acknowledgment that we regard phantasmata "as in a picture" (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 3). The picture-analogy is illuminating: just as a painting presents an appearance that is simultaneously real as an artifact and referential as a likeness, so the phantasma occupies a dual status—it is both a present object of contemplation (a θεώρημα) and a likeness (an εἰκών) of something absent. White reinforces this point by cautioning that although "imagination" is often the closest English approximation, "its post-Aristotelian connotations are extremely inappropriate for rendering Aristotle's phantasia," since the Greek term encompasses a broader cognitive range than the modern concept of creative fancy (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, pp. 12–14). Papachristou similarly leaves the word untranslated, recognizing that translating φαντασία as "imagination" risks importing misleading associations (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 9–10). For virtual-reality phenomenology, this dual character of the phantasma—present image and absent referent—precisely mirrors the structural ambiguity of the virtual object, which is perceptually given yet ontologically elsewhere. 

## 3. Phantasia and Memory: The Temporal Dimension of the Image The relationship between phantasia and μνήμη introduces the temporal dimension essential to understanding how images function not merely as present appearances but as bearers of pastness. Memory, for Aristotle, is a state or affection conditioned by the lapse of time and directed exclusively at the past; yet it depends constitutively on phantasia, since the phantasma serves as the medium through which the absent past is made cognitively available. Frede's observation that the wider integration of perceptual and rational faculties approaches something like a modern sense of consciousness is instructive here, for "aisthesis (in the wider sense) is then charged with the deliverance of the universal" (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 8). This widened sense of perception encompasses the memorial function, since the retention and recognition of phantasmata enables the soul to move from particular sensory episodes to the stabilization of universal concepts over time. White's analysis further clarifies that phantasia occupies an intermediate position between the immediacy of sensation and the abstractness of thought, precisely because phantom images retain sensory qualities while being temporally displaced from their originating perceptions (White, *The Meaning of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anime, III, 3-8*, pp. 12–14). The representational puzzle at the heart of this account—how the soul recognizes a present image as a likeness of an absent thing without already possessing access to the absent original—constitutes what we may call the memorial paradox of phantasia, a tension that Aristotle acknowledges but never fully resolves. Heidegger's broader phenomenological reading, wherein phantasia amounts to a making-present-to-itself of the world, suggests that this temporal displacement is not a deficiency but a constitutive feature of human cognitive life (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 149). The voluntariness of phantasia—its being "up to us," as Aristotle initially claims—is complicated by precisely the memorial case, since dreams and involuntary not all phantasiai are subject to deliberate control, a point to which subsequent chapters on deliberative phantasia and habituated phantasia will return. 

## 4. O'Gorman captures this tension by observing that *De Anima*'s discussion of phantasia illuminates the ambivalence in Aristotle's treatment of λέξις in *Rhetoric* Book 3, "because phantasia, while integral to cognition, is vulnerable to distortion and error" (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 4). Phantasia, unlike doxa, does not entail the assertion of truth or falsity; one may entertain a phantasma—viewing it, as Aristotle says, as one views a painting—without thereby committing oneself to any belief about the world. Frede underscores this by noting that the III.3 that phantasia is "up to us"—unlike supposition—is subsequently undermined within the chapter itself, since dreams are manifestly not under voluntary control and phantasiai can nonetheless be true or false (Frede, *The Cognitive Role of Phantasia in Aristotle*, p. 3). This complication reveals a productive tension: phantasia shares with doxa the capacity for truth and falsity, yet differs from it in lacking the commitment structure of genuine belief. Burke's treatment of rhetoric and imagination similarly illuminates this boundary, for the term "imagination" risks being dismissed as "overly psychologistic and extraliterary in its origins" (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 97–99), a caution that applies equally to translating phantasia as mere subjective fancy. Heidegger's emphasis on rhetoric's orientation toward κρίσις—"a definite decision in the sense of a δόξα"—further clarifies that the rhetorical function of phantasia consists precisely in moving an audience from uncommitted appearance toward committed judgment (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 124). The grades of phantasia thus become salient: sensory phantasia, which remains close to perceptual appearance, operates beneath the threshold of doxastic commitment; deliberative phantasia, which involves calculative reasoning and comparison, approaches doxa without collapsing into it. This graduated structure will be explored in full in the chapter on deliberative phantasia and its relationship to practical reasoning.
